html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Explain how intellectual property law limits what data AI may train on, and who owns outputs
  • Explain how nondiscrimination law reaches hiring, credit, housing and insurance AI
  • Explain how consumer-protection law treats unfair and deceptive AI claims and practices
  • Explain how product-liability law treats AI defects, including the new EU rules

2II.B.1: Explain how intellectual-property law applies to AI

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Understand, so the depth is Understand. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

Running case

Training Data, Hiring Results and a Marketing Claim

  • Helios's support assistant learned from help-center articles, some written by third parties
  • The hiring tool selects one group of applicants at a clearly lower rate than another
  • Marketing wants to call the assistant always accurate; it once gave a customer a refund window that does not exist
  • Jonas Weber, Head of Legal and Privacy, asks which laws beyond privacy are now in play

How Intellectual Property Law Meets AI

  • Copyright: protects creative works, so it bears on training data and on outputs that copy
  • Patents: protect inventions; courts and offices have required a human inventor
  • Trade secrets and confidentiality: protect model weights, prompts and data; leaks to public tools destroy secrecy
  • Trademarks and likeness: protect names, logos and personal identity against confusing or deceptive AI outputs
  • Contracts and licenses (website terms, dataset and model licenses) can limit data use even where law would allow it

Exam tip

For an IP question, first name the right being used (copyright, trade secret, license), then ask whether use is allowed.

Training Data: Copyright, Mining Exceptions and Opt-Outs Beyond the BoK

  • US: fair use, decided case by case on four factors: purpose and character, nature of the work, amount used, effect on the market (17 U.S.C. 107)
  • EU: text and data mining exceptions exist, but a rightsholder can reserve its rights
  • General-purpose model providers need a copyright policy that honors reservations (AI Act Article 53(1)(c)) and a public training-content summary (Article 53(1)(d))
  • Website terms, licenses and scraping rules can limit use even where an exception exists
  • Governance: license where needed, record sources and reasoning, honor opt-outs

Exam tip

Public availability is not permission: a question about scraped data asks for a license, an exception, or both, and for records.

Outputs: Who Owns What AI Makes? Beyond the BoK [Verify live]

  • Copyright needs human authorship: purely AI-generated material is not protected, while human-written parts and creative selection, arrangement or editing can be
  • The US Copyright Office released its report on copyrightability on 29 January 2025; prompts alone were not enough for authorship
  • Patents: an AI cannot be the inventor; humans who contribute to an invention can be
  • Infringing outputs: a model can reproduce protected text or images, so the user or the company may face a claim
  • Contracts decide the rest: vendor terms say who owns outputs and whether the vendor indemnifies for infringement claims
  • As of 27 October 2026: courts and offices are still refining these rules; check current authority
Exam tip

If no human contributed creative expression, there may be no copyright to own; the contract still allocates use and risk.

Licenses, Trade Secrets and Confidentiality Beyond the BoK

Area What to watch in AI
Open-source licenses permissive licenses allow wide reuse; copyleft licenses can require sharing derived code on the same terms
Model licenses open weights are not always open source; use restrictions, attribution and field-of-use limits
Dataset licenses permitted purposes (research only, non-commercial) and attribution duties
Trade secrets model weights, prompts and training recipes; reasonable secrecy measures are required
Confidential data staff pasting client or personal data into public tools can breach contract and destroy secrecy
  • Helios: an approved-tools list, license review for every model and dataset, and a rule against pasting confidential data into unapproved tools
Exam tip

Read the license: open weights do not mean unrestricted commercial use.

Where the Courts Stand Beyond the BoK [Dates] [Verify live]

Matter Point to know
Thomson Reuters v. Ross (Third Circuit, 29 September 2026) first federal appellate decision on fair use in AI training; the tool was not generative; the court did not hold training is always infringing
Bartz v. Anthropic (settled for USD 1.5 billion, approved 20 July 2026) training on lawfully acquired books was held fair use; keeping a library of pirated copies was not
Overall no controlling appellate ruling on generative AI training; outcomes depend on the facts, the source of the data and market harm
  • As of 27 October 2026: these cases are fast-moving and rest on secondary reports; treat them as illustrations, not settled law
Exam tip

The safe answer is that fair use is fact-specific: where data came from and what harm the use does to the market both matter.

3II.B.2: Explain how nondiscrimination law applies to AI

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Understand, so the depth is Understand. The course has 2 practice questions on this indicator.

Two Theories of Discrimination

  • Disparate treatment: treating people differently because of a protected characteristic, such as race, color, religion, sex or national origin (Title VII)
  • Disparate impact: a neutral practice that falls harder on a protected group; unlawful if it is not job related and consistent with business necessity, or if a less discriminatory alternative exists
  • In AI, proxies (a postal code, a gap in work history) can cause impact without using the characteristic
  • Laws also cover age (Age Discrimination in Employment Act, ADEA) and disability (Americans with Disabilities Act, ADA)

Exam tip

If the tool never sees the protected characteristic but the results differ, think disparate impact.

Measuring Adverse Impact: The Four-Fifths Rule

  • Selection rate: the share of a group's applicants who are selected
  • Impact ratio: the lower group's rate divided by the highest group's rate
  • A ratio below four-fifths (80%) is generally treated by federal agencies as evidence of adverse impact (29 CFR 1607.4(D), the Code of Federal Regulations)
  • It is a rule of thumb, not a safe harbor: smaller gaps can still be unlawful, and larger ones may not be
  • Example: 50% against 30% gives 0.6; 40 of 100 against 36 of 100 gives 0.9

Exam tip

Compute the lower rate over the higher rate; a result under 0.8 flags review, a result above does not clear the tool.

Employment: Screening Tools and the Vendor's Role [Verify live]

  • Employers answer for the tools they use to screen, rank or reject applicants
  • Vendors can be drawn in: in Mobley v. Workday, a US court let claims proceed on the theory that an AI hiring vendor can act as an agent of its employer customers
  • On 16 May 2025 the court allowed an age-discrimination collective to start
  • Disability: tools that screen out disabled applicants, or fail to offer reasonable accommodation, raise ADA risk
  • Age: tools that learn from past hires can copy age patterns (ADEA)
  • Governance: test for adverse impact before and after launch, keep human review, ask the vendor for validation evidence, document the job-relatedness of each criterion
  • As of 27 October 2026: the case was still pending; check its status
Exam tip

Buying a screening tool does not move the employer's responsibility for its effects.

Credit, Lending, Housing and Insurance

  • Credit and lending: ECOA and Regulation B require notice of action within 30 days of a completed application, with specific principal reasons; saying only that the applicant failed a credit score is insufficient (12 CFR 1002.9)
  • Housing: the Fair Housing Act covers tenant screening, pricing and ad delivery, including disparate impact
  • Insurance: state regulators police unfair discrimination in underwriting and rating variables
  • Credit reports: accuracy and adverse-action duties apply to scoring built on consumer reports (Fair Credit Reporting Act, FCRA)
  • A complex model does not excuse the duty to give specific reasons

Exam tip

For credit AI, the question is often whether the adverse-action notice gives specific reasons.

Nondiscrimination Beyond the US, and Managing the Risk Beyond the BoK

  • EU equality law bans direct and indirect discrimination by race, employment and gender, and in access to goods and services; indirect discrimination is the EU's term for a neutral practice with a disparate effect
  • The GDPR requires fair processing, and the AI Act asks high-risk providers to examine data for bias (module 6)
  • A governance routine: define the groups and the metric, test before launch, retest after changes, mitigate, document, and keep human review
  • Vendors: require bias-test evidence, ask what groups were tested, and reserve audit rights
Exam tip

Indirect discrimination in the EU and disparate impact in the US describe the same idea.

4II.B.3: Explain how consumer-protection law applies to AI

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Understand, so the depth is Understand. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

Unfair and Deceptive Practices: Section 5 and State Laws

  • Section 5 of the FTC Act makes unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce unlawful (15 U.S.C. 45(a)(1)); states have similar laws
  • Deception: a claim or omission likely to mislead reasonable consumers about something material
  • Unfairness: a practice that causes or is likely to cause substantial injury that consumers cannot reasonably avoid and that is not outweighed by benefits (15 U.S.C. 45(n))
  • Remedies can include orders, penalties and deletion of data or models built on improperly obtained data
  • The EU has unfair-commercial-practices law with the same aims

Exam tip

Deception is about what you said; unfairness is about what you did.

AI Washing and Claims About AI Beyond the BoK [Verify live]

  • AI washing: claiming a product uses or is powered by AI when it does not, or overstating what it can do
  • Capability claims such as accurate, unbiased, human-level or safe need substantiation before they are made
  • The FTC launched Operation AI Comply in September 2024 and has continued case-by-case enforcement against deceptive AI claims
  • Fake reviews, undisclosed bots and invented endorsements produced with AI are deceptive too
  • Helios: the claim that the assistant is always accurate cannot be substantiated, so it should be dropped or qualified
  • As of 27 October 2026: enforcement priorities shift; the principle does not
Exam tip

If a marketing claim about AI cannot be backed by evidence, the legal risk is deception, whatever the technology.

Chatbots, Dark Patterns and Data Practices

  • Chatbots: presenting a bot as a human, or hiding that a person is talking to AI, can mislead
  • Dark patterns: interface designs that steer or trap users, such as hidden cancellation, can be unfair or deceptive
  • Data practices: promising privacy or security and then using data to train models is a broken promise
  • Wrong outputs: if a customer relies on a wrong answer, the company's statements and disclaimers matter
  • Controls: disclose AI use, test claims, keep records of substantiation, give human escalation, and review marketing for AI statements
Exam tip

Disclosure does not cure a harmful design, and a disclaimer does not cure a false claim.

5II.B.4: Explain how product-liability law applies to AI

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Understand, so the depth is Understand. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

Product Liability Basics: Three Kinds of Defect

  • Strict liability for defective products can apply without proof of fault in many jurisdictions
  • Manufacturing defect: the product departs from its intended design
  • Design defect: the design itself is unreasonably dangerous
  • Failure to warn: inadequate instructions or warnings about risks
  • Claims can also rest on negligence and on contract warranties
  • Whether software is a product has been unsettled in US courts; the EU has settled it by statute

Exam tip

Match the facts to the defect type: departs from design, bad design, or missing warning.

AI Examples of Each Defect

Defect AI example
Manufacturing a pipeline error ships a corrupted model that behaves differently from the tested one
Design a triage model is built so that it systematically under-ranks a symptom
Warning no instructions on the tool's limits, or no warning that outputs may be wrong
  • Who answers: the manufacturer or provider, and sometimes suppliers and deployers
  • Updates and learning matter: a system can become defective after release
  • Evidence is hard to get; documentation, logs and testing records are the defense
Exam tip

Documentation helps both ways: it proves due care, and its absence suggests a design or warning failure.

The New EU Product Liability Directive Beyond the BoK [Dates] [Verify live]

  • Entered into force on 8 December 2024; applies to products placed on the market from 9 December 2026, which is also the transposition deadline
  • All types of software are covered, including AI systems
  • Manufacturers can be liable for defects at release and those that arise through updates, upgrades or machine learning
  • A product is defective if it lacks the safety a person is entitled to expect
  • Disclosure of evidence can be requested where proportionate and necessary, which eases the claimant's burden of proof
  • As of 27 October 2026: Member States are still transposing; check national laws

Exam tip

The Directive makes software, including AI, a product for liability, and the producer's duty continues through updates.

Liability Beyond Defects: The Withdrawn AI Liability Proposal Beyond the BoK [Dates]

  • The Commission proposed an AI Liability Directive on 28 September 2022 to ease claims for harm caused by AI
  • It withdrew the proposal, announcing it on 11 February 2025, citing no foreseeable agreement
  • Liability for AI harm now runs through the Product Liability Directive, national negligence and contract law, and sector rules
  • Contracts allocate risk between vendors and customers: warranties, indemnities, liability caps and insurance (module 12)
  • Governance: keep testing and monitoring records, give clear warnings, and review vendor terms and insurance
Exam tip

Do not assume a dedicated AI liability law: liability follows product, negligence and contract rules, plus the AI Act's duties.

6Exam Q&A

6.1 Practice questions (one best answer, or select exactly the number the question asks for)

S1A company plans to train a model on text scraped from public websites. Which TWO steps best manage copyright and data-use risk? (Select TWO.)

  • ACheck whether the sites reserve rights against mining or restrict reuse in their terms
  • BAssume that publicly accessible content may be used for training and needs no review
  • CRely on a documented legal basis, such as a license or exception, and keep source records
  • DRemove copyright notices from the scraped text before it is used for training the model
  • ETrain first and review the sources after the model has been released to the public
Show the answer

Answer: A, C. Rights reservations and site terms can restrict use, and the company needs a documented basis, such as a license or an applicable exception, with records of sources. Public availability is not permission, stripping notices does not help, and reviewing after release is too late.

S2A screening tool never uses race or sex as an input, yet it rejects a much larger share of one group. Which theory of discrimination most directly applies?

  • ADisparate treatment, because a difference in outcomes shows that people were treated differently on purpose
  • BDisparate impact, because a neutral practice has a disproportionate effect that may not be justified
  • CNeither theory, because discrimination law applies only when a protected attribute is an input
  • DFraud, because the tool hides how it reaches its decisions from the people it screens
Show the answer

Answer: B. A facially neutral practice that falls harder on a protected group is a disparate impact issue, and the employer must be able to show the practice is job related and consistent with business necessity. A protected attribute need not be an input.

S3A screening tool selects 40 of 100 male applicants and 36 of 100 female applicants. What does the four-fifths rule of thumb indicate?

  • AThe ratio is 0.9, so the rule does not flag adverse impact, though that is not a safe harbor
  • BThe ratio is 0.9, so the tool is proven lawful and needs no further testing for bias
  • CThe ratio is 0.4, so the rule flags adverse impact and the tool must be withdrawn from use by the company
  • DThe ratio is 1.1, so the rule flags adverse impact against the male applicants as a group of people
Show the answer

Answer: A. The lower rate (36%) divided by the higher rate (40%) is 0.9, above 0.8, so the rule of thumb does not flag adverse impact. It is not a safe harbor: smaller differences can still be unlawful, and testing continues.

S4Helios wants to advertise its customer assistant as always accurate, although it has given wrong answers. Which area of law most directly makes the claim a risk?

  • ACopyright law, because the assistant's answers may resemble the help-center articles it learned from
  • BTitle VII, because the claim could affect how applicants view the company as an employer
  • CConsumer-protection law on unfair or deceptive practices, because the claim cannot be substantiated
  • DProduct-liability law, because the advertisement itself is a defect in the assistant's design
Show the answer

Answer: C. A capability claim that cannot be backed by evidence is a deceptive practice under consumer-protection law. The other areas of law are not engaged by the advertising claim itself.

S5An AI triage tool is built so that it systematically ranks a serious symptom below less serious ones, and patients are harmed. Which kind of product defect does this most closely resemble?

  • AA manufacturing defect, because the tool departs from the design its builders intended and tested
  • BA design defect, because the way the product was designed makes it unreasonably dangerous to use
  • CA failure to warn, because the tool did not tell the users that it was designed by software engineers
  • DNo defect, because the tool is software and its ranking was learned from data rather than designed
Show the answer

Answer: B. When the design itself is unreasonably dangerous, the defect is one of design. A manufacturing defect departs from the intended design, a warning defect concerns missing instructions, and the new EU rules expressly cover software, including AI.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
IP check the right to use data (license, exception, opt-out); human authorship for outputs; licenses, trade secrets and confidentiality
Nondiscrimination disparate treatment and disparate impact; the four-fifths rule of thumb; employment, credit, housing, insurance; the vendor does not carry the employer's duty
Consumer protection deception and unfairness; substantiate AI claims; disclose bots
Product liability manufacturing, design and warning defects; EU rules cover software and updates
